title: The largest small octagon
contribution: Settles the first open case of Graham's 1975 conjecture: among unit-diameter octagons the maximum area 0.726867 is attained by Graham's conjectured configuration, proven by reducing to 31 diameter-graph configurations, solving the conjectured one with the QCQP branch-and-cut and eliminating the other 30.
problem_entry: Graham (1975) solved the hexagon and conjectured the optimal shape for even n >= 8; the octagon is the first open case (p. 3).
key_idea: Extend Graham's hexagon method: linear thrackleations (Woodall) leave 31 configurations; solve configuration (31) exactly as a 10-variable QCQP (z* ~ 0.726867, accuracy ~1e-5) and certify the other 30 cannot exceed 0.7268 (pp. 3-14).
assumptions: Convex octagons of unit diameter (p. 3); certificate relies on solver accuracy ~1e-5 (p. 7) and on heptagon/hexagon optima 0.7198/0.6750 rounded up (pp. 10-11).
proof_devices: exhaustion over 31 diameter-graph configurations from Woodall's linear-thrackle theorem (p. 3)
one-angle analytic upper bound 2B(theta)+cos theta sin theta+(1-sin theta)/2 checked by a plot, eliminating 23 configurations (pp. 9-10)
incumbent-cutoff infeasibility: QP with area >= 0.7268 plus angle bounds from smaller-polygon optima shown infeasible by the exact solver (pp. 10-11)
necessary optimality conditions (perpendicularity) derived by moving one vertex at a time, added to relaxations of the incumbent configuration so the exact solver can prove infeasibility (pp. 12-14)
experiments: none beyond solver runs; configuration (31) took more than 100 hours (p. 12)
positioning: Extends Graham's thrackleation-plus-optimization method to n = 8 (pp. 3, 14); only 5 references, two of them Audet's thesis and the QCQP branch-and-cut (p. 15).
writing: Short note with a one-sentence contribution in the abstract (p. 2), figure-driven case analysis, one-paragraph conclusion without limits or future work (p. 14).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated (p. 14); unstated: §4.1 relies on a plot and the proof on solver tolerance ~1e-5 (pp. 7, 10); 2.78% here vs 2.79% in S108 (rounding).

method_links.note: Proposer/certifier split in exact optimization: the conjecture proposes the incumbent configuration; all other cases must be certified unable to beat it.
Thesis-era QCQP branch-and-cut code reused as the instrument that settles a 1975 conjecture (reused research code, not a maintained product).
Add objective >= incumbent and prove infeasibility for each non-incumbent case.

title: Optimization tools for engineering design using surrogate functions
contribution: AFOSR final report (grant F49620-01-1-0013, Dec 2000-Nov 2003) of the Dennis (PI)-Audet (CoPI) project: announces MADS as lifting GPS's fixed-direction restriction, documents NOMAD C++ cycle 5 and its industrial users, and lists publications, talks and ExxonMobil/Boeing transition projects.
problem_entry: Engineering design with expensive simulations and surrogates (p. 1); the research problem named is GPS's reliance on a fixed finite set of directions to which convergence results are tied (p. 4).
key_idea: MADS explores a set of directions dense in the whole space and generalizes GPS (p. 4); NOMAD C++ cycle 5 offers GPS/MADS, a cache, filter, bound barrier with conforming directions, user surrogates and LH search (pp. 3, 5).
assumptions: not applicable (grant report: no model or theorem)
experiments: Anecdotal only: ExxonMobil tanker problem (<=15 min vs over a day, p. 3); 4-variable catalytic reactor fit, GPS beats gradient method and MADS faster than GPS (p. 5); Kelley's public well-location problems (pp. 5-6); Boeing planform with surrogates (pp. 16-17).
positioning: Positions NOMAD for DAKOTA integration (pp. 3, 5) and Boeing's Design Explorer (p. 16); special issue of Optimization and Engineering co-edited with L.N. Vicente (pp. 1, 3).
writing: Grant-report register: claims of an exceptionally productive period (p. 1), bullet lists of outputs, and transition projects each with status, blocking reason and contact (pp. 14-17).
limits_future: MADS to replace GPS, earlier papers to be recast in the book (p. 5); projects delayed by ExxonMobil internal funding (p. 15) and Boeing priorities (p. 16); Le Digabel and Zghal starting PhDs on MADS extensions (p. 4).

method_links.note: NOMAD C++ already carries research features to UTRC/ExxonMobil; a user problem (well-bore trajectory) is logged as a future algorithm application; Dennis's talk Optimization Tech Transfer is a Two-Way Street.
MADS motivated by GPS convergence results known not to hold; Audet's 2003 talks titled First Order Optimality Conditions Tied to Local Differentiability.
User-defined surrogates and Latin hypercube searches added to NOMAD as search-type features.
The public benchmark is another group's (Kelley's well-location problems); the group's own industrial problems (Boeing nozzle, ExxonMobil casing) are not released.

quotes.text: MADS is much more flexible, and allows us to show the convergence results that we always wished for in GPS, but knew did not hold.
Previous approaches could sometimes hold up the process for over a day, while NOMAD has never needed more than 15 minutes to solve an instance of the problem.

title: Generalized pattern searches with derivative information
contribution: Uses available (possibly approximate or partial) derivative information to prune ascent directions from the GPS poll set, reducing the worst-case Poll cost from n+1 evaluations to one with the implicit direction set {-1,0,1}^n, while proving that GPS convergence results are unchanged.
problem_entry: User question: how to use derivatives where available (p. 1); target is the worst-case O(n) Poll cost, continuing Lewis-Torczon (pp. 1-2); engineering codes give cheap inexact gradients (p. 2).
key_idea: Change only the Poll: prune directions with d'grad f > 0; poll from the never-constructed rich set D = {-1,0,1}^n, which any nonzero vector prunes to a singleton (Thms 2-3, p. 9); Search left for global exploration (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: A1 f_X = f + indicator available (f may be nonsmooth/discontinuous), A2 rational constraint matrix, A3 iterates in a compact set (p. 13); approximate gradients need only sign agreement on the largest components (Def. 6, p. 10).
proof_devices: Davis's positive-spanning characterization (Thm 1, p. 3) and pruning number rho(D) with rho(D) >= |D|/2 for positive bases (Prop. 1, p. 7)
completion of the surviving direction by all directions with negative inner product, positive spanning checked by a two-case construction (Thm 2, pp. 8-9)
Clarke-quotient argument with a pruned-direction case: a direction counts if polled or pruned infinitely often, since d'grad f(x_k) > 0 bounds the quotient below by zero (Thm 6, pp. 13-14)
epsilon-approximation to the large components: sign agreement suffices to prune to a singleton (Def. 6, Thm 4, p. 10)
experiments: NOMADm, Poll-only (empty Search), 8 poll strategies on CUTE problems (text: seven strategies, 20 problems; Table 1 has 21 rows), stop at Delta <= 1e-4 or 50,000 evaluations, f and grad-f evaluations counted separately, perturbed starts for fairness; plus a 2-D example showing a 2-point random Search finds the global minimum (pp. 14-18).
positioning: Continues Lewis-Torczon's reduction of per-iteration cost (p. 2); builds on the Audet-Dennis GPS analysis and tightness report (pp. 13-14); relates surviving directions to Byrd-Tapia l1/l_inf gradients (pp. 6, 9).
writing: Explicit hedges on what the experiments mean (p. 2); flags 'a major point of this paper' (p. 7); clarifies the ambiguous term 'pruned set' (p. 5); credits referees for a shorter proof of Prop. 3 (p. 18).
limits_future: No time saving if the gradient costs about n evaluations (p. 18; p. 2); pruned polls may end at different, sometimes worse minimizers (PALMER1, p. 18); future: derivatives in the Search, e.g. Hermite interpolants (pp. 2, 4).

method_links.note: Search/Poll division explicit (Search decides global quality), but the performance idea goes into the Poll and is admitted because the proof is redone with pruned directions counted as polled.

Ladder relative to local smoothness at the limit (Lipschitz -> Clarke; strict differentiability -> grad f = 0; linear constraints + conforming -> KKT); A2 flagged as needed; liminf Delta_k = 0 not strengthenable by the tightness example.
Evaluation currency with f and grad-f counted separately, fairness perturbations, unflattering PALMER1 reported; but same-family variants only, with an explicit disclaimer.

title: An exact method for fractional goal programming
contribution: First exact approach to general fractional goal programming: a counterexample shows optima need not be vertices, a localization theorem bounds the optimal face, and a reformulation to a linearly-objectived QCQP is solved by the group's branch-and-cut (and a complementarity-aware variant) on random instances with up to 14 fractional objectives.
problem_entry: All published methods are heuristic (local NLP or vertex enumeration), and a two-variable example with a non-vertex optimum shows vertex enumeration can fail (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Introduce denominator variables and deviation variables d+, d- to obtain a QCQP with linear objective and LP-derived bounds; solve with qp, or frac which fixes the complementary deviation to zero when branching forces the other positive (p. 3).
assumptions: Bounded polyhedron X; denominators strictly positive on X (p. 1); bounds from LPs (p. 3).
proof_devices: two-variable counterexample: optimum (2,2) not at a vertex (p. 2)
localization (Prop. 1): freeze the deviation sign pattern at an optimum, apply a Carrizosa-Plastria corollary to get an optimal face of dimension <= m-1, then count objectives at target (pp. 2-3)
complementarity d+ d- = 0 automatically satisfied at the optimum, exploited as a branching rule (p. 3)
experiments: Random instances with planted attainable targets and nonzero optimum; m in {6,10,14}, n in {5,10,15}, 30 per cell; mean/std CPU seconds; factors: redundant constraint (4), simulated heuristic warm start, qp vs frac (pp. 4-6).
positioning: Positions against the heuristic fractional goal programming literature (Kornbluth, Steuer, Romero) and reuses a Carrizosa-Plastria localization technique (pp. 1-2).
writing: Presents itself as a note exploring the practical applicability of a recent algorithm (p. 1); four remarks sketch extensions (p. 6).
limits_future: High variance of solve times (p. 6); heuristic baselines not run (pp. 4-6); extensions to m = 1, piecewise convex penalties, quadratic ratios and posynomials only sketched (p. 6).

method_links.note: Exact method as certifier of a heuristic's solution; certification cost measured with a simulated warm start.
Minimal counterexample to a solution-method shortcut (optimum at a vertex), then a correct weaker localization result.
Factorial design on random instances with mean and std; CPU-time currency; no external baseline.
Reuse of the group's qp branch-and-cut code, slightly modified to exploit complementarity.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: qp of Audet-Hansen-Jaumard-Savard reused here; same code settles the octagon in S037 and S108

transferable: Linearize a sum of ratio-deviation terms by making each denominator a variable and splitting deviations into d+ and d-, giving a linear objective with bilinear constraints (p. 3).
Branching rule from implied complementarity: when branching forces one member of a complementary pair above zero, fix the other at zero (p. 3).
Simulate a good heuristic by re-running the exact method with the known optimum as incumbent; the difference measures the cost of proving optimality (p. 4).
Generate random instances with a planted, separately attainable target per objective and discard trivial instances with optimal value 0 (p. 4).

quotes.text: However, only heuristic procedures are suggested in the literature on the field.
Given a solution produced by a heuristic method, the algorithm can be used to either confirm its global optimality or to show that it is not optimal by finding the true global solution.

title: Quatre petits octogones
contribution: French expository account (text read: MATAPLI no. 80, 2006) of how the authors solved the four first open small-octagon problems (maximal area, maximal perimeter, and both for equilateral octagons) by combining diameter-graph case analysis with two exact global solvers, with the history of the problems and a list of new open problems.
problem_entry: Four questions on small n-gons; odd n, n = 4, even n not a power of 2 (perimeter) and n = 6 (area) are solved, so the first open cases are all octagons (pp. 2-9).
key_idea: Reduce each problem to 31 diameter-graph configurations and settle each with global optimization: RLT branch-and-cut for QCQP (area, equilateral perimeter) or interval branch-and-bound IBBA (perimeter) (pp. 10-15).
assumptions: Convex unit-diameter polygons (p. 2); analytic closed forms obtained with Maple under an assumed symmetry axis, stated as such (pp. 15, 19).
proof_devices: relaxation-saturation: solve configuration 10 (a relaxation of 29) and observe the extra constraint active at the optimum (p. 14)
first-order optimality conditions plus angle bounds added as constraints eliminate configuration 10 in 0.12 s (p. 14)
rounding-controlled interval arithmetic guaranteeing all digits of the maximal perimeter 3.1211 (p. 15)
closed forms for regular small polygons yield non-monotone sequences and another proof of Reinhardt's even-n result (pp. 17-18)
experiments: Computational records only: >100 h on a SUN-SPARC 20 for area configuration 31 (p. 12); 3 h, 12 h and 44 h on a 30-PC cluster for the perimeter (p. 14); 45 s for the equilateral-perimeter QP (p. 15).
positioning: Places the work in a 1922-2005 history (Reinhardt, Vincze, Graham, Bieri, Mossinghoff, Yuan) and critiques Graham's omitted symmetry proof (pp. 6-8).
writing: Popular-science register in French: rhetorical questions (p. 1, p. 17), the playful club of 'octogonistes' (p. 10), anecdotes, and closing open problems (pp. 18-19).
limits_future: Open: decagon (area), 16-gon (perimeter), octagons of maximal width (conjectured solution 0.9776 unproven) and equilateral width entirely open (pp. 18-19); equilateral area regular only verified for n = 4, 6, 8 (p. 16).

method_links.note: Hypothesis audit applied to geometry literature: Graham's omitted symmetry proof, Bieri's unproven symmetry assumption, Reinhardt's buried epilogue; own symmetry-assuming solutions labelled.
Two exact solvers from the coauthors' theses and papers (RLT branch-and-cut; IBBA) reused as instruments across four problems.

title: Enumeration of all the extreme equilibria in game theory: bimatrix and polymatrix games
contribution: Formulates bimatrix and polymatrix game equilibria as the feasible set of a mixed 0-1 LP with data-derived big-L constants and gives Ex-MIP, the first algorithm enumerating all extreme equilibria of polymatrix games, tested up to 14x14 bimatrix and 13x13x13 three-player games and compared honestly with the group's faster bimatrix-only EEE.
problem_entry: Equilibria form unions of polytopes, so enumerate their vertices; EEE handles bimatrix games only (bilinear approach), and no complete enumeration existed for more than two players (pp. 1, 3-4, 9, 22).
key_idea: Linearize complementary slackness of each player's LP with binaries and big-L; enumerate extreme feasible solutions per binary pattern with a principal tree over binaries, secondary trees fixing positive continuous variables to zero, and no-good cuts (pp. 5-6, 10-12, 16-17).
assumptions: Normal-form games with finite strategy sets; polymatrix payoffs are pairwise sums (pp. 2, 8); no nondegeneracy assumption stated (pp. 4-18).
proof_devices: valid big-L from payoff ranges (max - min), proved by bounding alpha and A_i y between extreme entries (Props 2.1, 3.1, pp. 5, 10-11)
completeness of Ex-MIP by principal + secondary branching (Thm 5.1, pp. 17-18; sketch citing a nonexistent Proposition 5.2)
iterated strict-dominance elimination terminating in at most M^2 iterations (Prop. 4.1, p. 15); weak dominance excluded as unsafe (p. 15)
experiments: C++ + CPLEX 6.0; 10 random games per cell, payoffs uniform on [0,10], densities 0.12-1; mean/std of nodes, CPU time and number of extreme equilibria; bimatrix 5x5-14x14 vs EEE, 3-player 3x3x3-13x13x13 (pp. 20-21).
positioning: Extends the group's EEE (bimatrix only) to polymatrix games via MIP; cites Keiding and von Stengel bounds and the LCP line (Howson, Yanovskaya) (pp. 3-4, 9).
writing: Formulation-first with short propositions; claims a first for polymatrix games and concedes slower times on bimatrix (p. 22); several cross-reference slips (pp. 5, 6, 17, 21).
limits_future: Slower than EEE on larger, denser bimatrix games (pp. 21-22); polymatrix time grows exponentially (p. 22); future: equilibrium refinements (p. 1).

method_links.note: Competitor is the group's own state of the art on its home ground and is conceded faster; identical equilibrium counts as correctness cross-check; CPU-time currency.
Outside DFO: only provably lossless preprocessing (strict dominance) is allowed; weak dominance excluded because it may lose equilibria.
L constants from payoff ranges answer the admitted difficulty of choosing them.
